_note: Draft content for expert review (child protection officer, IZU volunteer, teacher). Non-graphic by design. Short sentences and everyday words. correctAnswer: A = Safe, B = Uncomfortable, C = Unsafe. Each age group has its own deck: level 1 cards are for ages 6-8 (Explorer), level 2 cards for ages 9-11 (Guardian), so a child who grows into the older path meets new situations. "night": the story happens after dark. "trick" (9-11): the warning sign the child names after sorting the card.

items.title: A hug from Grandma
items.question: Grandma gives you a big hug, and you like it. How is this?
items.feedback: Hugs you like from family are safe. You can always say no to a hug.
items.deeper: Even with people you love, a hug is your choice. A wave is fine too.

items.title: Too much tickling
items.question: Your cousin keeps tickling you after you said "stop". How is this?
items.feedback: Your "stop" matters. Say it again, loudly. Tell a grown-up if they don't stop.
items.deeper: A game stops being fun when one person wants to stop. Your "stop" counts in games too.

items.title: A touching secret
items.question: A neighbour says, "Let's keep a touching secret. Don't tell your parents." How is this?
items.feedback: Touching is never a secret. Say NO, move away and tell a grown-up you trust. It is never your fault.
items.deeper: People who ask for touching secrets know it is wrong. Telling is never breaking a promise.

items.title: At the health centre
items.question: A nurse checks your tummy. Your mum is with you. How is this?
items.feedback: Nurses and doctors may check your body to keep you healthy, with a parent there.
items.deeper: A body check is safe when it is for your health, a parent is with you, and the nurse says what they are doing.

items.title: Sweets from someone new
items.question: Someone you don't know offers you sweets to come with them. How is this?
items.feedback: Never go with someone you don't know. Say NO, go somewhere safe and tell a grown-up.
items.deeper: Some people use sweets, money or rides to get children alone. Safe grown-ups never ask you to go without telling your family.

items.title: Standing too close
items.question: A classmate stands very close and won't move when you ask. How is this?
items.feedback: Ask again, move away, and tell your teacher if it keeps happening.
items.deeper: Feeling uncomfortable matters. Use your words first, then ask a teacher for help.

items.title: High-five from your teacher
items.question: Your teacher gives you a high-five for a good answer. How is this?
items.feedback: A high-five for good work is a safe, friendly touch.
items.deeper: A safe touch is short, open, and where others can see. You would be happy to tell your family about it.

items.title: A message online
items.question: An older person you met online asks for photos of you and says to keep it secret. How is this?
items.feedback: Never send photos to people who want secrets. Stop replying and show a grown-up.
items.deeper: Only known online, asking for photos, asking for secrets: three warning signs. Block them, keep the messages and show a grown-up. You are not in trouble.

items.title: Gifts with a catch
items.question: A family friend gives you gifts and says you owe them a "special secret". How is this?
items.feedback: Gifts should never come with secrets. Tell a grown-up you trust, even if the person is nice.
items.deeper: This is called grooming: being nice and giving gifts, then asking for secrets. A gift does not mean you owe them anything.

items.title: Sitting on a lap
items.question: An adult you know wants you to sit on their lap. You don't want to. How is this?
items.feedback: You can say "No, thank you" and sit somewhere else. Your body belongs to you.
items.deeper: Saying "no, thank you" politely is not rude, even to adults you know.

items.title: Pictures on a phone
items.question: An older cousin shows you pictures on a phone of people with no clothes on. They say it's a secret. How is this?
items.feedback: This is not okay, even from family. Move away and tell a grown-up you trust.
items.deeper: Showing these pictures to a child is a kind of abuse, even with no touching. It is never your fault that you saw them.

items.title: A friend's worry
items.question: Your friend says an adult touches her in a way she doesn't like. She asks you not to tell. How is this?
items.feedback: Your friend is not safe. Tell a grown-up you trust. That is how a good friend helps.
items.deeper: Some secrets are too big for children. Telling a grown-up gets your friend help.

items.title: A kiss hello
items.question: Your uncle says you must kiss him hello, and you don't want to. How is this?
items.feedback: You can wave or shake hands instead. A kind hello doesn't need a kiss.
items.deeper: Grown-ups who care about you will accept a wave. If someone gets angry, tell a parent.

items.title: Late after school
items.question: It's dark and you are late leaving school. A driver you don't know says, "Your mum sent me. Get in!" How is this?
items.feedback: Never get into a car with someone you don't know, even if they say your parents sent them. Say NO, go back to school and ask your teacher to call home.
items.deeper: A grown-up who collects you is someone your family told you about first. Agree a family password: no password, no ride.

items.title: Lost after dark
items.question: It's getting dark at the market and you can't find your mum. A lady selling fruit, with her own children, offers to phone your mum. How is this?
items.feedback: If you are lost, stay where people can see you and ask a mum with children or a shopkeeper to call your family. Wait there, and never go off with anyone.
items.deeper: Learn your family's phone number by heart, so a helper can call them for you.

items.title: Someone following you
items.question: It's dark. You are walking home and a grown-up you don't know keeps following you. How is this?
items.feedback: Go quickly to a bright place with people, like a shop, and tell a grown-up there. Then tell your family.
items.deeper: Trust your uh-oh feeling. After dark, walk home with a friend or a grown-up you trust, on busy, bright roads.

items.title: The coach asks first
items.question: At netball practice, the coach asks, "May I move your hands to show you the throw?" Your whole team is there. How is this?
items.feedback: The coach asked first, for a reason, with everyone there. That is safe. You can still say no.
items.deeper: Safe grown-ups ask first, explain why, stay where others can see, and never ask for secrets.

items.title: A video call at night
items.question: It is late at night. Someone you met in a game asks you to turn on your camera and keep it secret. How is this?
items.feedback: Never turn on your camera for someone you met online. Don't reply, and tell a grown-up you trust.
items.deeper: People online are not always who they say. Asking for secret video or photos, late at night, is a big red flag.

items.title: A friend asks first
items.question: You win a race. Your friend asks, "Can I give you a hug?" and you say yes. How is this?
items.feedback: Your friend asked, and you said yes. That is safe. Asking first is how friends show respect.
items.deeper: It works both ways: ask before you hug others too, and their no is always okay.
